body:
What is a patent?

A patent is a statutory intellectual property right granted by the government for an invention. It gives the patent holder, called the patentee, the exclusive right to prevent certain unauthorised commercial and other acts involving the patented invention within the country that grants the patent.

An invention may concern a new product, such as a device or material, or a new process, such as a method of manufacturing a product. However, every new idea or useful improvement does not automatically qualify for patent protection. The invention must satisfy the legal tests of patentability.

Under Section 2(1)(j) of the Patents Act, 1970, an invention is a new product or process involving an inventive step and capable of industrial application.

Why does the patent system exist?

Inventors may invest time, money and effort in developing technical solutions. If competitors could immediately reproduce every successful invention, inventors might have less incentive to undertake costly research. Patent protection creates a limited period during which the inventor or another lawful patent holder can control the specified uses of the invention.

In return, the applicant must disclose sufficient technical information to explain the invention. This information becomes available through the patent system, allowing others to learn from the disclosed technology. Once the patent term ends, the invention is no longer protected by that patent, although other independent legal rights may still matter.

The system therefore seeks to balance temporary exclusive rights with public disclosure and eventual wider use of technical knowledge.

A patent is not ownership of every idea

Consider a person who thinks of reducing water wastage through an improved automatic tap. The broad idea of saving water is not, by itself, a patentable invention. A particular technical product or process developed to solve the problem may qualify if it is new, involves an inventive step, has industrial application and is not excluded by law.

The same distinction applies to scientific discoveries. Discovering a natural phenomenon is different from inventing a qualifying technical application based on scientific knowledge.

Important characteristics of patent rights

Patents are territorial

An Indian patent gives rights in India. It does not automatically prevent others from using the invention in another country. Protection abroad ordinarily requires compliance with the patent laws and procedures of the relevant countries. Filing under the Patent Cooperation Treaty can assist with international patent applications, but it does not create a single worldwide patent.

Patents are limited in duration

In India, the normal patent term is 20 years from the filing date, subject to the provisions of the Act and payment of required renewal fees. The term is not calculated as 20 years from the date of grant.

Patents provide a right to prevent, not automatic permission to manufacture

A patent holder may prevent others from carrying out acts covered by the granted patent. However, holding a patent does not automatically give permission to manufacture or sell the product. Other valid patents, safety approvals and applicable laws may still restrict its use.

Indian patent law: essential background

The principal legislation is the Patents Act, 1970, supported by the Patents Rules, 2003, as amended. The Indian Patent Office administers the examination and grant system under the Office of the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks.

A major change occurred in 2005, when India extended product-patent protection to fields including pharmaceuticals, food and chemicals. Such inventions must still satisfy patentability requirements and statutory exclusions.

Prelims focus

  • The Patents Act, 1970, is India's principal patent legislation.
  • Section 2(1)(j) defines an invention as a new product or process involving an inventive step and capable of industrial application.
  • A patent is a territorial right; an Indian patent protects the invention in India.
  • The normal Indian patent term is 20 years from filing, subject to statutory conditions.
  • The 2005 amendment enabled product patents in fields including pharmaceuticals.
  • Trap: A patent is not an unconditional licence to manufacture or market an invention.

[Sources: Government of India, The Patents Act, 1970, Sections 2(1)(j), 48 and 53, Intellectual Property India website (consulted 14 November 2026); Intellectual Property India, Basics of Patents and History of Indian Patent System (consulted 14 November 2026); Press Information Bureau, Patent Filing Services, 18 March 2013.]

title: Patents: Meaning, Purpose and Legal Protection

body:
When does an invention qualify for a patent?

Patentability depends on more than usefulness. Under Indian law, an invention must satisfy novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability. It must also fall outside the exclusions specified by Sections 3 and 4 of the Patents Act, 1970.

These requirements operate together. Passing one test cannot compensate for failing another.

Novelty: the invention must be new

An invention is novel if its claimed subject matter has not already been disclosed in a way that anticipates it before the relevant priority date. Earlier information is called prior art.

Prior art may include earlier patent publications, scientific articles, technical manuals, public demonstrations and other qualifying disclosures or uses. Information from outside India can also be relevant. An invention does not become new merely because it is being introduced in India for the first time.

For example, if a particular water-filter mechanism has already been fully disclosed in an earlier public patent document, a second person cannot obtain a valid patent for the same mechanism merely by giving it a new name.

Publication before filing

Publicly disclosing an invention before securing the relevant filing or priority date can destroy its novelty. Indian law contains limited statutory exceptions for certain disclosures, but there is no general rule that every inventor may publish freely and then claim a patent at any time within the following year.

Inventive step: the invention must not be obvious

Novelty and inventive step are different. An invention may contain a feature not previously described in exactly the same form yet still be an obvious modification of existing technology.

Section 2(1)(ja) defines an inventive step through 2 connected requirements: the feature must involve a technical advance over existing knowledge or have economic significance, or both; and it must make the invention not obvious to a person skilled in the art.

A person skilled in the art is a hypothetical person possessing ordinary knowledge and skill in the relevant technical field. The test asks whether the claimed invention would have been obvious to such a person in light of existing knowledge, rather than whether it impresses a person unfamiliar with the subject.

Novel but potentially obvious

Suppose a known storage container is made in a slightly different decorative colour. Even if the exact colour arrangement is new, this change would ordinarily not establish an inventive technical advance. Conversely, a genuinely non-obvious mechanism that reduces leakage through a new functional arrangement may potentially satisfy the inventive-step requirement, provided the other legal tests are met.

Industrial applicability: the invention must be capable of practical use

Section 2(1)(ac) provides that an invention is capable of industrial application when it can be made or used in an industry. This requirement distinguishes an implementable technical solution from something that exists only as an unsupported idea.

The expression is not confined to large factories. A qualifying invention may concern a useful manufacturing method, instrument or industrially usable product. However, industrial applicability does not override statutory exclusions. For example, methods of agriculture or horticulture are excluded under Section 3(h), even though agriculture is economically productive.

The role of the priority date

A priority date is the legally relevant date against which earlier disclosures are assessed for a particular patent claim. When a claim is properly supported by an earlier provisional specification, that earlier filing may establish its priority. Material first disclosed in a later complete specification may have a later priority date.

This is why the order of events matters. Filing an adequately drafted application before publicly revealing the invention can be important for preserving patentability.

How the tests work together

RequirementCentral questionTypical reason for failure
NoveltyWas the claimed invention already disclosed?An earlier publication anticipates the claim.
Inventive stepWould the invention be obvious to a skilled person?The change is merely an obvious modification.
Industrial applicationCan the invention be made or used in industry?The proposal has no practical industrial application.
Statutory eligibilityIs the subject matter excluded by law?The claim falls under Section 3 or 4.

Novelty asks whether it was already known. Inventive step asks whether it would have been obvious. Industrial applicability asks whether it can be made or used in industry.

Prelims focus

  • Section 2(1)(j) identifies novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability as the core features of an invention.
  • Section 2(1)(ja) defines inventive step using technical advance or economic significance, together with non-obviousness.
  • Section 2(1)(ac) concerns capability of being made or used in industry.
  • Prior art is not limited to information originating in India.
  • Sections 3 and 4 exclude certain subject matter even where other criteria appear satisfied.
  • Trap: Newness alone does not establish inventive step.

[Sources: Government of India, The Patents Act, 1970, Sections 2(1)(ac), 2(1)(j), 2(1)(ja), 2(1)(l), 3, 4 and 11, Intellectual Property India website (consulted 14 November 2026); Intellectual Property India, Basics of Patents, sections on novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability (consulted 14 November 2026).]

pictures.alt: A claim must satisfy novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability and statutory eligibility together; passing one cannot offset failing another.
pictures.caption: All the patentability requirements must be satisfied.

title: The Essential Tests of Patentability

body:
Why are some discoveries and innovations not patentable?

Even a useful technical development may be ineligible for a patent because Indian law excludes particular categories of subject matter. Section 3 lists matters that are not considered inventions for the purposes of the Patents Act, while Section 4 restricts patentability of inventions relating to atomic energy.

These exclusions protect important distinctions between discovery and invention, prevent inappropriate monopolies over existing knowledge and preserve specified public interests.

Discoveries, natural substances and abstract ideas

Section 3(c) excludes the mere discovery of a scientific principle, the formulation of an abstract theory, and the discovery of a living thing or non-living substance occurring in nature.

For example, identifying a naturally occurring microorganism or observing a previously unknown natural property does not, by itself, amount to a patentable invention. A separately developed technical product or process involving that knowledge must be assessed under all applicable legal requirements.

Section 3(a) also excludes frivolous inventions and claims obviously contrary to well-established natural laws.

Important exclusions under Section 3

ProvisionExcluded subject matterKey distinction
Section 3(a)Frivolous claims or claims obviously contrary to natural lawsA scientifically impossible assertion is not a qualifying invention.
Section 3(b)Inventions contrary to public order or morality, or causing specified serious harmSerious prejudice to health, life or the environment is relevant.
Section 3(c)Mere discoveries, scientific principles and abstract theoriesDiscovering nature is not the same as inventing a technical solution.
Section 3(d)Specified new forms, properties or uses of known substances and other subject matter without the required conditionsA new form of a known substance must meet the statutory enhanced-efficacy requirement.
Section 3(e)Mere admixture producing only an aggregation of known propertiesSimply combining known substances so that the mixture shows only an aggregation of their known properties is insufficient.
Section 3(f)Mere arrangement or duplication of known devices working independently in known waysPutting existing devices together does not necessarily create an invention.
Section 3(h)Methods of agriculture or horticultureAn agricultural method is excluded even if practically useful.
Section 3(i)Specified methods of treating or diagnosing humans or animalsA treatment method is distinct from a potentially patentable medical device.
Section 3(j)Plants and animals, including seeds and varieties, subject to the stated microorganism exceptionMicroorganisms are not covered by this particular blanket exclusion.
Section 3(k)Mathematical or business methods, computer programmes per se and algorithmsA computer programme as such is excluded.
Sections 3(l)–3(o)Creative works, mental acts, game rules, presentation of information and integrated-circuit topographyOther forms of intellectual property may protect some of these subjects.
Section 3(p)Traditional knowledge or mere aggregation or duplication of known traditional propertiesExisting community knowledge cannot simply be presented as a new invention.

Section 3(d): the distinction between a new substance and a new form

Section 3(d) is especially significant in the context of medicines and chemical substances. It excludes the mere discovery of a new form of a known substance if the new form does not result in enhancement of the known efficacy of that substance. It also excludes the mere discovery of a new property or new use of a known substance, and the mere use of a known process, machine or apparatus unless the known process results in a new product or employs at least 1 new reactant.

The provision does not prohibit every pharmaceutical invention. It requires the actual claimed invention to satisfy the statutory criteria, including the special conditions applicable to known substances.

Section 3(i): medical methods and medical products

Indian law excludes specified processes for medicinal, surgical, curative, preventive, diagnostic and other treatment of human beings, along with comparable processes concerning animals.

This must not be confused with a general prohibition on medical technology. A novel medical instrument or pharmaceutical product is not excluded merely because it relates to healthcare. Its patentability depends on the claimed subject matter and all applicable statutory requirements.

Section 3(j): plants, animals and microorganisms

Section 3(j) excludes plants and animals in whole or in part, including seeds, varieties and species, and essentially biological processes for producing or propagating plants and animals. The provision contains an exception for microorganisms.

This exception does not mean that every microorganism is patentable. A naturally occurring microorganism merely discovered in nature remains subject to Section 3(c), and an alleged invention involving a microorganism must still meet novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability and other legal requirements.

Section 3(k): software and algorithms

Section 3(k) excludes a mathematical or business method, a computer programme per se and algorithms. The words per se mean that a computer programme as such is excluded. The presence of software in a wider technical invention does not, by itself, settle patentability; the substance of the claimed invention must be examined.

Traditional knowledge and protection against unjustified patents

Traditional knowledge includes information developed and maintained within communities over generations. Examples may concern the established properties or uses of plants and other biological resources.

Under Section 3(p), an invention that is effectively traditional knowledge, or merely duplicates known properties of traditionally known components, is not patentable. This principle is important in India because extensive knowledge of plants, agriculture and biological resources existed long before modern patent applications.

The term biopiracy is used in discussions of unauthorised or unfair exploitation of biological resources or associated traditional knowledge. Patent objections based on existing traditional knowledge help prevent wrongly granting exclusive rights over information that was already known.

Section 4: inventions relating to atomic energy

Section 4 provides that patents shall not be granted for inventions relating to atomic energy falling within the restrictions specified under the Atomic Energy Act, 1962. It is a separate statutory exclusion from the categories in Section 3.

Patentability has 2 levels: an invention must satisfy the positive tests of novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability, and it must avoid the statutory exclusions. Satisfying the positive tests does not cancel Section 3 or Section 4.

Prelims focus

  • Section 3(c) excludes mere discoveries of naturally occurring substances and scientific principles.
  • Section 3(d) contains special restrictions concerning known substances and enhanced efficacy.
  • Section 3(i) excludes specified medical treatment and diagnostic processes.
  • Section 3(j) excludes plants, animals and seeds, with a stated exception concerning microorganisms.
  • Section 3(k) excludes computer programmes per se, algorithms and mathematical or business methods.
  • Section 3(p) concerns traditional knowledge; Section 4 concerns atomic-energy-related inventions.
  • Trap: The microorganism exception in Section 3(j) does not make a mere natural discovery patentable.

[Sources: Government of India, The Patents Act, 1970, Sections 3 and 4, Intellectual Property India website (consulted 14 November 2026); NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter 12, Biotechnology and Its Applications, Section 12.4, Ethical Issues, consulted in GPSC_35 compendium, PDF pages 238–239.]
